title: One form, many sights
hook: ek moorat anek darsan: one form seen in countless ways (Jaap, roaaval)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gobind, the Sustainer, and your line, generous and infinite. Did you give a little more than felt necessary? Today, Jaap slows into longer lines, and plays with one and many. Day three hundred forty-seven.

Hold a glass prism up to a window. One beam of plain white light goes in. Out the other side comes a whole spread of color, red, orange, green, blue, violet, splashed across the wall. Nothing was added. The colors were in the light all along; the glass just let you see them separately. Then put a second prism the right way round, and the colors can fold back into a single beam of white. Many from one, one from many. Jaap Sahib has a stanza that works exactly like that prism. Today: one form, many sights.
screen: `ONE BEAM INTO A PRISM.` → `A SPREAD OF COLORS ON THE WALL.` → `FOLDED BACK INTO WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here Jaap moves into a meter called roaal, with longer, rolling lines, and one stanza opens like this: ek moorat anek darsan, keen roop anek. Ek is one. Moorat is form or likeness. Anek is many, countless. Darsan is a sight, a glimpse, the word Sikhs use for seeing something holy, as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple. So: one form, countless sights; You made forms beyond number. Then comes the line many Sikhs love: khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek. Khel is play, a game. Having played the play, beyond all play, at the end, again One. Think about what that does. Earlier, Jaap called the One aroop, formless. Now it says the One shows itself in countless forms. That isn't a contradiction. It's the prism. The light has no color of its own, and yet every color is the light. Sikh scripture often calls the world the One's khel, the play, the great unfolding game: every person, every animal, every grain of sand one more color from the same beam. And then the stanza does the second prism. At the end, it all folds back. Again, One. This matters on an ordinary day because it changes how you look at people. The rude driver, your sister, the stranger on the bus, the friend you think you know completely: each one a different color from the same light. Same source, countless sights. And none of them is the whole picture of anyone.
screen: `EK MOORAT: ONE FORM.` · `ANEK DARSAN: COUNTLESS SIGHTS.` · `KHEL: THE WORLD AS THE ONE'S PLAY.` · `ANT KO PHIR EK: AT THE END, ONE.` · then, large: `ONE, SEEN MANY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a friend with fresh eyes. Picture someone you know well. Now see them from angles you usually don't: as a small child, as their parents see them, as their coworkers do, at three in the morning, on their best day. Let each picture be one color from the prism. Then let them fold back into the one person you love. Same friend, many sights. Breathe with that. If you pray, you can say ek moorat anek darsan softly. The bell holds the time.
One form. Ek moorat anek darsan: one form, seen in countless ways, playing the great play and at the end, again One.
Your line: one, seen many ways. Today, with one person who annoys you, try to see one more color in them than you usually do. Day three hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 347 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ENDER AND SUSTAINER OF ALL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this roaal stanza of Jaap Sahib each morning, and the idea of the world as the One's khel, play, runs through Sikh scripture and kirtan.

like light through a prism: no color of its own, yet every color is the light.

as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple.
the stanza ends with everything staying many
khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek: at the end, again One.

fork.setup: the One has made forms beyond number and played the great play. what does the stanza say happens at the end?
options: the play starts over the same way.
fork.reveal: ant ko phir ek: having played the play, beyond all play, at the end it all folds back into One.

original.note: Gurmukhi: moorat, form or likeness; ek moorat, one form, as in akaal moorat in the Mool Mantar.

trapdoor: what you thought: one form, many sights means God looks different to different people.
what it means: the One shows itself in countless forms, the world is its play, and at the end all is again One.
what a scholar hears: the roaal stanza (around 81) moves from ek to anek and back (ant ko phir ek), a Gurbani pattern of the world as the One's khel.
